articles.body: One of the things candidates search before an online hiring assessment is whether they can cheat it. We have a page per assessment vendor answering that, 56 of them, and the answer on every single one is no. That is an unusual content cluster to build, because the thing that normally differentiates pages in a cluster, the conclusion, is fixed. 56 pages, one verdict. Everything interesting is in how they are keyed and how the index renders. Keyed to the instrument, not the buyer The first decision was what the unit is, and the alternative was tempting because we already had the data for it: a page per employer. /cheating/<provider> 56 pages, one per assessment vendor Whether an assessment can be cheated is a property of the instrument, not of the company that bought it.

articles.title: CSS Container Style Queries: Let the Parent Set the Theme
articles.excerpt: Every design system eventually grows a modifier class problem. The card needs a dark version for the footer, a compact version for the sidebar, and a "highlighted" version for the pricing page. So you…
articles.body: Every design system eventually grows a modifier class problem. The card needs a dark version for the footer, a compact version for the sidebar, and a "highlighted" version for the pricing page. So you add .card--dark , .card--compact , .card--featured , and then you need a dark compact card, and then the button inside the card also needs to know it's on a dark background. Now the class has to be threaded through three components, or you're writing selectors like .card--dark .button . Container size queries solved half of this in 2023: components could finally react to the space they're given instead of the viewport. The other half, reacting to the context they're placed in, became Baseline Newly available in May 2026 when Firefox 151 shipped support for container style queries.

articles.title: Your Rate Limiter Is a Stampede at the Window Boundary
articles.excerpt: The fixed window lets double the traffic through at the boundary, the distributed counter is an agreement problem in disguise, and the token bucket is the honest answer. The page came at 00:00:37 on a…
articles.body: The fixed window lets double the traffic through at the boundary, the distributed counter is an agreement problem in disguise, and the token bucket is the honest answer. The page came at 00:00:37 on a Tuesday. The database was falling over and the rate limiter's dashboard said everything was fine. Limit: 5,000 requests per minute. Busiest minute on record: 4,800. The limiter was telling the truth. The database was dying anyway. Somewhere around 23:59:59, twenty-five hundred requests landed in the last second of one window. At 00:00:01, twenty-three hundred more landed in the first second of the next. Each window reported "under the limit." The database received forty-eight hundred requests in about two seconds. That is the stampede. It is not a bug in your limiter.

articles.title: Parse the destination before deduplicating a resource link
articles.excerpt: A useful project directory needs two separate answers: where will this link navigate, and what counts as the same resource? Treating those questions as one string-replacement operation creates subtle…
articles.body: A useful project directory needs two separate answers: where will this link navigate, and what counts as the same resource? Treating those questions as one string-replacement operation creates subtle mistakes. A substring such as agprolabs.com can appear inside an unrelated hostname. Removing every query parameter can merge two different resources. Changing the destination while counting it can quietly alter what the reader opens. I maintain AGProLabs, AliGurtuna.com and Babamın Şiir Defteri. Their resource pages include a TradingView review journal , a health-tool directory and a literary-review archive . These are distinct projects and readers. This example implements a small editorial URL policy for a resource menu across those three owned domains.

articles.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
articles.excerpt: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to…
articles.body: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements .

articles.title: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.excerpt: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.body: Aussie composer Mick Gordon is highly regarded for his experimental approach to musical composition. For 2013's Killer Instinct he employed a kangling, a Tibetan instrument traditionally carved into a human femur or tibia, to build a theme for the skeletal Spinal character out of actual bones. For 2016's Doom he famously sampled real chainsaw noises to pull off the unique guitar riffs that elevated the game's soundtrack into a heavy metal masterpiece. However, when asked if he's considered incorporating any form of generative AI into his creative process, Gordon doesn't mince his words. To paraphrase the late Meatloaf, Gordon will do anything to create a great soundtrack, but he won't do that .

articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.
